title: Microwave-assisted synthesis of copper-based electrocatalysts for converting carbon dioxide to tunable syngas
abstract: Copper (Cu)-based materials for efficient CO2 conversion to adjustable syngas are reported. We employ an energy-efficient microwave-assisted route to synthesize copper/copper oxides with different structures and morphologies. The initial oxidation state of the copper on the surface significantly influences the performance of the materials in the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR). On the as-prepared material surface, a high content of Cu2O improves the selectivity toward CO and consequently the catalyzed CO2RR produce a syngas with a low H2/CO ratio, while the CuO performs badly. In particular, Cu2O particles with a cubic shape show the highest selectivity for the CO formation. The superior catalytic activity of the Cu2O cubes for the CO2RR is attributed to the surface roughening under potential, which offers abundant electrochemically active sites and facilitates mass transport. 10.1002/celc.201901730 A cc ep te d M an us cr ip t ChemElectroChem This article is protected by copyright. sections.text:
Copper (Cu)-based materials for efficient CO2 conversion to adjustable syngas are reported. We employ an energy-efficient microwave-assisted route to synthesize copper/copper oxides with different structures and morphologies. The initial oxidation state of the copper on the surface significantly influences the performance of the materials in the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR). On the as-prepared material surface, a high content of Cu2O improves the selectivity toward CO and consequently the catalyzed CO2RR produce a syngas with a low H2/CO ratio, while the CuO performs badly. In particular, Cu2O particles with a cubic shape show the highest selectivity for the CO formation. The superior catalytic activity of the Cu2O cubes for the CO2RR is attributed to the surface roughening under potential, which offers abundant electrochemically active sites and facilitates mass transport.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Electrochemical conversion is considered to be a very attractive approach for CO2 valorization, since it can be developed based on other existing technologies such as polymer electrolyte membrane (PEM) electrolyzers, PEM fuel cells, solid oxide fuel cells and so on. Furthermore, it can be powered by electricity generated from renewable energy sources and allows CO2 reduction to value-added chemicals under mild conditions. This technology, although being very promising, confronts many challenges due to the high stability of CO2 molecules, high reaction energy barriers, slow kinetics for CO2 electroreduction, and low selectivity toward a specific target product due to multiple parallel reactions occurring at the electrode surface. Hence, electrocatalysts are essential to activate the chemically stable CO2 in order to obtain higher reaction rates with lower energy consumption. Among many products, formic acid (HCOOH) and carbon monoxide (CO) are the only technoeconomically viable products that have been obtained up to now with relevant productivities [1]. CO is highly desired in the industrial sector, since its mixture with hydrogen (H2), namely synthetic gas or syngas, can be further converted to oxygenates and hydrocarbons through the Fischer-Tropsch process [2-4]. According to experimental and theoretical studies, gold (Au) and silver (Ag) are considered
to be the best metal catalysts for converting CO2 to CO [5，6]. Instead, copper (Cu) shows
unique features of electrochemically converting CO2 to a range of chemicals including alcohols and hydrocarbons [7，8], while its selectivity for CO is low. However, by tuning the
morphology and surface composition of the Cu-based catalysts, it is possible to adjust the selectivity for CO and to obtain syngas with various H2/CO ratios [9]. Moreover, as

compared to the nanostructured Au and Ag catalysts for the same function, Cu-based catalysts are much less expensive and more suitable for pratical applications. In this work, we synthesized Cu-based materials through a simple and fast route with microwave irradiation, using copper sulphate as Cu precursor and ethylene glycol as reducing agent. Under the microwave radiation at 180 °C, Cu 2+ ions were reduced, forming Cu nanoparticles. An oxide shell was then formed on the metallic particle, due to the exposure to air. With the addition of Sn 4+ or Sn 2+ ions to the copper precursor, the oxidation state of particles was changed as well as the morphology. In addition, Cu2O cubes were formed in the presence of a certain amount of Sn 4+ . When adding Sn 2+ , Cu particles had a significantly reduced size and were covered by a layer of CuO. Various electrochemical techniques were applied in order to evaluate the activity and selectivity of these electrocatalysts toward the CO2RR. It is revealed that the H2/CO ratio of syngas can be easily tuned by adopting different catalysts.

sections.heading: 2.1 Materials
sections.text: Tin(II) chloride dihydrate (SnCl2·2H2O, 99.9 %), tin(IV) chloride pentahydrate (SnCl4·5H2O, 98 %), copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate (CuSO4·5H2O, 99.0 %), sodium hydroxide (NaOH, 98 %), potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3, 99.7 %), ethylene glycol (EG, 99.8 %), Nafion ® 117 solution (5 wt.%) and isopropanol were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. Unless otherwise specified, all the materials were used as received.

sections.heading: 2.1 Synthesis of copper-based catalysts
sections.text:

sections.heading: 2.2 Preparation of electrodes
sections.text:
To prepare the electrode, 10 mg of synthesized Cu catalyst (Cu-1, Cu-2, Cu-3, Cu-4, Cu-5 or
Cu-6), 1.0 mg of acetylene carbon black (CB, Shawinigan Black AB50), 90 l of Nafion®
117 solution and 320 l of isopropanol were well mixed and sonicated for 30 min until a
uniform slurry was obtained. The slurry was then coated onto a carbon paper (GDL; SIGRACET 28BC, SGL Technologies). The obtained electrode was dried at 60 °C overnight to evaporate the solvents. The mass loading of Cu catalyst is about 3.0 mg cm -2 .

Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscopy (FESEM, ZEISS Auriga) was used to evaluate the morphology of the as-prepared material and electrodes. TEM analysis was performed with a Tecnai G2 F20 S-TWIN (FEI) equipped with a field emission gun (FEG), operated at 200 kV. For TEM characterization the catalysts were dispersed and sonicated in ethanol, and then deposited on TEM grids. X-ray diffraction (XRD) was performed in Bragg-Brentano symmetric geometry by using a PANalytical X’Pert Pro instrument (Cu-Kα radiation, 40 kV and 30 mA) equipped with an X’Celerator detector. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was carried out by using a PHI 5000 VersaProbe (Physical Electronics) system. The X-ray source was a monochromatic Al Kα radiation (1486.6 eV). Spectra were analyzed using Multipak 9.7 dedicated software. All core-level peak energies were referenced to C1s peak at 284.5 eV and the background contribution, in high resolution (HR) spectra, was subtracted by means of a Shirley function. The elemental analysis was carried out via Inductively Couple Plasma Optical Emission (ICP-OES), with an iCAP 7600 DUO (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The RF power of the plasma, the nebulizer gas flow, the coolant gas flow and the auxiliary gas flow were 1150 W, 0.5 L/min, 12 L/min, 0.5 L/min, respectively. Samples were weighted and digested in a flask with 10 % of aqua regia overnight, filled up at volume with Milli-Q and filtered using a 0.45 µm PTFE filter before reading them with the instrument. Ar gas was used as Internal Standard and the R 2 value of the calibration for the Sn and Cu elements (189.99 λ, 324.75- 224.70 λ, radial mode respectively) was 0.999.

EIS measurements were performed at various potentials from -0.2 V to -0.8 V with an AC signal of 10 mV of amplitude and 10 -1 - 10 4 Hz frequency range in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 aqueous solutions. Chronoamperometric (CA) measurements were carried out by using a CHI760D electrochemical workstation in order to analyze the products of the CO2RR. The CA experiments were conducted in a custom-made two-compartment cell with a proton exchange membrane (Nafion™ Membrane N117, Sigma-Aldrich) as the separator. The volume of each side was 40 ml with 15 ml of headspace. A Ag/AgCl (1 mm, leak-free LF-1) was used as the reference and a Pt foil as the counter electrode. The working electrode was a catalyst (Cu-1, Cu-3, Cu-5 or Cu-6) coated carbon paper with a geometric area of 1.5 cm 2 . 0.1 M KHCO3 aqueous solution was used as electrolyte. For CV and CA experiments, the potential was corrected by compensating the ohmic potential drop, of which 85 % by the instrument (iRcompensation) and 15 % by manual calculation. Gas-phase products were analyzed on-line with a micro gas chromatograph (µGC, Fusion®, INFICON) equipped with two channels with a 10m Rt-Molsieve 5A column and an 8 m Rt-Q-Bond column, respectively, and micro thermal conductivity detectors (micro-TCD). The inlet of the µGC equipment was connected to the cathodic side of the electrochemical cell through a GENIE filter to remove the humidity from the gas. During the CA measurements, a constant CO2 flow rate of 20 ml min -1 was maintained to saturate the electrolyte and to carry out the gaseous products to the µGC. sections.heading: 3. Results and Discussion
sections.text:
3.1 Physical and chemical characterization
FESEM images of the synthesized Cu samples are shown in Fig. 1. It is evident that the morphologies of these samples are dependent on the precursor solutions. Only irregular particles were obtained when no Sn(IV) and Sn(II) salts were present in the precursor solution (Fig. 1a). The particles have a wide size distribution from a couple of tens to a few hundreds of nanometers. Adding Sn(IV) into the precursor solution promotes the formation of smaller particles and these small particles agglomerate significantly (Fig. 1b-d). Particles with a cubic shape increase in quantity with increasing the amount of Sn(IV) in the solution. When the Sn(IV) salt increases to 10 wt.% with respect to the Cu(II) one, cubic morphology becomes absolutely dominant (Fig. 1e). In addition, pores and channels are observed in the inner part of several imperfect cubes, as shown in the inset of Fig. 1e. Instead, when the Sn(II) was added into the precursor solution, the size of particles significantly decreases, as displayed in Cu-6 sample in Fig. 1f.

XRD patterns of Cu-based catalysts are shown in Fig. 2. The main peaks of the Cu-1 correspond to the reflections corresponding to (111), (200) and (220) planes of metallic Cu crystalline phase (Copper, JCPDS 00-004-0836). Two tiny peaks corresponding to (111) and (200) planes of Cu2O (Cuprite, JCPDS 00-005-0667) are also observed, giving evidence of a small quantity of Cu2O in the Cu-1 sample. Similar crystalline phases are observed on Cu-2, Cu-3 and Cu-4 samples. With increasing the amount of Sn(IV) in precursor solution, all peaks corresponding to the metallic Cu phase decrease in intensity while the related Cu2O diffraction peaks increase. When the percentage of Sn(IV) salt increased to 10 wt. % with respect to the Cu(II) precursor (sample Cu-5), it is interesting to note that all peaks are associated to Cu2O and in particular to the (110), (111), (200), (211), (220), (311) and (222) planes, while no peaks for metallic Cu are observed. Moreover, in this pattern, the diffraction peak intensity ratio of (111) and (200) surfaces is about 2.71, close to the value of 2.70 reported for a standard pattern of Cu2O with a cubic cuprite structure (Cuprite, JCPDS 00- 005-0667). XPS measurements have been performed on the Cu-1, Cu-3, Cu-5 and Cu-6 samples to investigate the chemical composition of their surface. From the survey spectrum (not reported), Cu, O and C are the main elements and trace of Sn is also detected in all these samples. The presence of C element could be attributed to the preparation of the sample or due to adventitious carbon. The ultra-low quantity of Sn is further confirmed by the ICP-OES analysis (Table 2). From these values, it is reasonable to assume that Sn exists at a negligible level in all the samples. Actually, due to the high pH (> 12.5) of the final solution, Sn element can be stabilized as HSnO2 - and as SnO3 2- (HSnO2 - /Sn, -0.79 V; SnO3 2- /HSnO2 - , - 0.69 V vs SHE) at 25 °C [10]. These anions are soluble in H2O or H2O/EG, which can explain why no Sn are considered in the final powder samples.

The Cu2p doublet region acquired in high resolution (HR) mode is shown in Fig. 3a. The Cu1, Cu-3 and Cu-5 samples show a typical structure related to the mixed oxidation states of Cu, including Cu(0), Cu(I) and Cu(II), while the Cu-6 sample displays a typical spectrum related to only Cu(II) [11]. The Cu2p peak is complicated to be deconvoluted due to both the presence and overlapping of several satellites and shake-up peaks for each oxidation state. In order to obtain more details, the Auger CuL3M4,5M4,5 region was also acquired (shown in Fig. 3b). The resulting modified Auger parameter is approximately 1849 eV for both Cu-1 and Cu-3 samples, which corresponds to the average oxidation state (AOS) of Cu(I) [12]. XRD results also reveal the coexistence of metallic Cu and Cu2O in the Cu-1 and Cu-3 samples, while CuO is absent, probably due to its low quantity or amorphous form. The Cu-5 sample also has an average oxidation state of Cu(I) on the surface, in agreement with the XRD result, and both analyses indicate a large amount of Cu2O. For the Cu-6 sample, the modified Auger parameter is about 1851.1, which is typical of Cu(II), indicating that its surface is mainly composed of CuO with a thickness of at least 5-10 nm (the sensible depth for XPS). Such a high amount of CuO was also identified and confirmed by XRD data (see Fig. 2). By summarizing, according to the Cu(II) satellite relative intensity and Cu2p3/2 FWHM, we can state that the Cu(II) abundance increases in such a way: Cu-1 < Cu-5 < Cu-3 < Cu-6.

TEM investigation was performed on Cu-1, Cu-5 and Cu-6, in order to further elucidate the structural properties of these samples. The BF-TEM in Fig. S1 shows that the structure of the samples Cu-1 and Cu-6, which consist of particles, is a core-shell structure, and gives comparative information both on particles size and shell thickness. The Cu-1 is composed of particles with a larger size and a thinner shell, as compared to the Cu-6. From HRTEM, the particles of Cu-1 sample consist of a large metallic Cu core and a polycrystalline 5nm-thick Cu2O shell (Fig. 4a). Similar with the Cu-1, the Cu-6 catalyst also shows a core-shell structure (Fig. 4c). However, the structure of Cu-6 has a relatively smaller core and a thicker shell. The shell is polycrystalline CuO with a thickness slightly larger than 10 nm, which can explain why only CuO is detected by XPS. The core can be either Cu or Cu2O as confirmed by FFT patterns, which is in agreement with the XRD analysis. The TEM investigation on Cu-5 catalyst is complicated by the thickness of the crystals, which makes them only partially transparent to the electrons. Therefore, HRTEM investigation was performed by studying different corners (TEM visible part) within the cubes, and not the central part, as shown in Fig. 4b and Fig. S1. The analyses performed on the corners suggest that these parts (at least 50 nm in thickness) of the cubes are monocrystaline Cu2O. No evidence of Cu and CuO has been found, in agreement with XRD result.

sections.heading: 3.2 Discussion on the formation of Cu-based catalysts
sections.text:
The abovementioned characterizations enable a deep understanding of the nature of the Cubased catalysts, which can further help to establish the formation process of various samples. When adding the alkaline solution 2 to the solution 1, a blue precipitate is firstly formed. With increasing the pH, a clear and dark solution is obtained. In an alkaline EG/H2O mixture Cu(II) exists as [Cu(OH)4] 2- or [Cu(C2H4O2)2] 2- complexes [13, 14]. We assume that the redox potentials of the Cu species (Cu(II), Cu(I) and Cu(0)) in EG/H2O follow the same order as that in the potential-pH diagram, which is theoretically valid only in aqueous solution. Previous studies have found that this assumption is valid for a wide range of noble metal cations [15, 16]. From the potential-pH diagram, the reduction potentials of the Cu species at a pH of 13 are as following: ECu(II)/Cu(I) = -0.09 V vs. SHE (R1) ECu(I)/Cu(0) = -0.27 V vs. SHE (R2) The reduction of the Cu(II) complexes follows two steps according to R1-R2. Initially, Cu(I) forms and then it gets further reduced to metallic Cu at high reaction temperature. The high temperature and high pH value are essential for yielding metallic Cu particles in EG, which is consistent with other reported works [17, 18]. When the temperature decreases to ambient

condition, the surface of Cu particles can be easily oxidized into Cu2O or CuO in air [19]. Hence, the Cu-1 sample is found to have a core of metallic Cu and a shell of Cu2O oxide. With adding Sn(IV) in the precursor, the percentage of Cu(I) increases with respect to Cu(0) in the samples. The oxidation grade increases with increasing the quantity of Sn(IV) in the precursor. When the SnCl4:CuSO4 weight ratio increases to 1:10 (Sample Cu-5), only Cu2O is formed. It is likely that the introduction of Sn(IV) can inhibit a further reduction of Cu(I). According to Zheng et al. [20], the Sn(IV) could adhere on the surface of Cu(OH), acting as a barrier between Cu(OH) and EG. Hence, the Cu(OH) can be stabilized instead of being further reduced by EG and then it turns to Cu2O. The addition of Sn(II) leads to the reduction of particles size. The nanosized particles are easier to be oxidized and thus the sample Cu-6 displays Cu/Cu2O in the inner layer and thick shell of CuO, as confirmed by XPS and TEM analyses. Besides the chemical composition, the morphology of the sample is also dependent on the precursor solution. As previously discussed, the addition of Sn(IV) and Sn(II) can lead to the reduction of particle size, in agreement with the literature [20, 21]. The particles, especially nano-sized ones, tend to agglomerate, which could be driven by surface energy reduction [22, 23]. It is worth noting that the Cu2O agglomerates have a cubic shape, distinct from other particles with mixed oxidations. However, pores and channels observed in the inner part of several cubes, as shown in the inset of Fig. 1e, rule out the single crystal structure of Cu2O agglomerates. These apparently contradictory results found a possible explanation in oriented-attachment mechanism that leads to the formation of meso-crystal from smaller nano-scale crystal seeds as already reported in Ref. [23, 24]. In our hypothesis EG, used as the bulk solvent, plays the role of a surfactant favoring the oriented packing of small Cu2O particles. It has been established that a major influence on the shape of the resulting mesocrystal is exerted by the morphology of the nanocrystal. By means of ab-initio simulations,

carried out in the framework of the Density Functional Theory (DFT), we predicted the nanocrystal shape. The DFT study of the clean Cu2O surfaces highlighted the higher thermodynamic stability of the (111) and (110) surfaces, in agreement with the literature, with respect to the (100) [25] (see SI, Fig. S2-S3 and Table S1). The corresponding Wulff’s construction would predict multi-faceted polyhedral crystallites at equilibrium. On the contrary our DFT simulations showed that a crucial role is played by the EG molecules that function as capping agent during growth. In effect, the binding energies of an EG molecule to the (110), (111) and (200) surfaces are -0.30 eV, -1.50 eV and -1.76 eV respectively (cf. Supporting Information). The highest binding energy with the (200) surface points at the higher stability of the {100} surfaces in presence of EG molecules, thus explaining the appearance of cubic-shaped Cu2O. Indeed, EGs while binding to the {100} surfaces inhibit the growth on those surfaces. On the contrary, the growth along the [111] and [110] directions is not hindered, so that the corresponding facets will eventually disappear.
3.3 Product analyses on the Cu-based electrodes
The electrocatalytic performance toward the CO2RR of various Cu-based electrodes was firstly studied by using CV in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 aqueous solution. CO2 gas was bubbled through the electrolyte for 30 min before CV tests and the same gas flux was maintained during the measurements. The current densities are normalized by both the geometric electrode area and the electrochemically active surface area (ESA) of the electrodes. The evaluation of the ESA values of the electrodes is deeply discussed in Fig. S4 and Table S2. A higher ESA value could indicate a higher amount of the reaction sites at the electrode. In general, the geometric current density represents the total activity of the electrode, while the specific current density (normalized by the ESA) displays the activity of the reaction sites. As shown in Fig. 5a, the Cu-5 and Cu-6 electrodes display higher geometric current densities compared to the Cu-1 and Cu-3 ones at each applied potential in

By comparing these samples, the Cu-1 electrode has a low total activity but a high specific activity, indicating that the Cu-1 catalyst has highly active reaction sites even though they are less abundant. The Cu-3 electrode displays a similar behavior with the Cu-1 one. In contrast, the Cu-6 electrode has a good total electrode activity but a poor specific activity, because it has most dense but less active reaction sites. On the Cu-5 electrode, both the total and specific activities are high, indicating its rich and active reaction sites. Even though the activities of the samples are evaluated, the selectivity for the CO2RR on each sample cannot be estimated from the CV curves since the CO2RR and HER occur simultaneously.

In order to investigate the performance of various electrodes for the CO2RR, CA measurements were carried out in a three-electrode two-compartment cell. As shown in Fig. 6a, the current densities decrease in the first 20 min due to the reduction of oxides at the electrodes. The reductive current density reaches 5.8 mA cm -2 at about -0.6 V and it increases with negatively shifting the applied potential (8.8 mA cm -2 at -0.7 V and 11.5 mA cm -2 at -0.9 V). Similar current densities are observed on other samples at each potential (see Fig. S5a, S6a and S7a). The production rates of H2 and CO were determined by µGC every 2 minutes. As shown in Fig. 6b, c, d, the CO yield on the Cu-5 sample reaches a quasi-constant value after 15 min of electrolysis and then it slightly decreases, while the H2 production rate increases with time. Other electrodes display a similar behavior (Fig. S5-S7). It is worth noting that the production rates of syngas at our electrodes are higher, as compared to other similar studies [26, 27]. To further investigate the stability behavior, 6 hours of electrolysis has been performed on the Cu-5 electrode at -0.7 V. As shown in Fig. 6e, the Cu-5 electrode maintains a quasi-steady current density. However, the selectivity for the CO formation drops down from 45 % to 32 %, while the FE for H2 yield increases to 57 % at the end of the test. This deactivation behavior could be due to the accumulation of carbonaceous species on the Cu electrodes during the CO2RR [28, 29]. Many studies also approve that the degradation of the CO2RR performance at the Cu electrodes are correlated to their morphological/structural evolution at negative potentials [30-32]. We studied the Cu electrodes after test and observed similar material evolutions. As shown in Fig. S8 and S9, most of the catalysts are reduced into metallic Cu and the surface of all the samples encounters potential-induced roughening during the CO2RR. Appropriate strategies must be put forward in order to preserve the structures of Cu electrocatalysts and to maintain their electrochemical performance during the CO2RR.

By comparison with the other samples Cu-1 and Cu-3, increasing the Cu2O content in the as-prepared catalysts increases the CO selectivity at each potential. Hence, by changing the Cu state, the H2/CO ratio of the syngas can be easily tuned. At all electrodes, H2 and CO are the main products at the tested potentials from -0.6 V to -0.8 V. At such potentials, the faradaic efficiency for the HCOOH remains about 10 %. No other liquid products, except HCOOH, are detected by HPLC, and no other gas-phase products, except H2 and CO, were detected neither expected, since the total faradaic efficiency for the three observed products are almost 100 %. More negative potentials (< -0.9 V) are not recommended for the syngas production on Cu-based electrodes, since other gas-phase products can emerge, which increase the impurity of the syngas [33- 35].

In order to understand why Cu-5 sample outperforms the other samples, EIS analysis has been carried out. Cu-1 and Cu-3 samples are analyzed for comparison. As an example, the Nyquist plots of the impedance acquired on Cu-5 electrode in CO2-saturated electrolyte at different potentials is shown in Fig. 9a. The experimental curves are characterized by a highfrequency (HF) arc which does not depend on the applied potential, a middle-frequency (MF) one which reduces its radius while negatively shifting the potential, and a low-frequency (LF) feature which appears at potentials equal or lower than -0.5 V [38]. The HF process accounts for the charge transport inside that catalyst layer, the MF one stands for the charge transfer at the catalyst/electrolyte interface, and the LF one is related to the mass diffusion into the electrolyte; the distance between the origin of axis and the HF arc depends on electrolyte and contact resistances [39]. In order to quantify the different contributions to the total catalyst impedance, the experimental curves were fitted through the equivalent electrical circuit shown in the inset of Fig. 9a, composed by the series resistance Rs (electrolyte and contact resistances), the Rt//Ct parallel (HF process), the Rct//Cdl parallel (LF process) and the Warburg impedance Zw (LF process) [33]. sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
Cu-based materials have been prepared with a simple experimental approach and carefully characterized by employing several advanced surface analysis techniques. The obtained particles in most cases have a core-shell structure, in which the core is metallic Cu and the shell is Cu2O or CuO. Even though both oxide shells are reduced to metal and both surfaces encounter potential-induced roughening during the electrocatalysis operation, the Cu particles derived from Cu2O appear to be more active for catalyzing the CO2RR to CO. A thick Cu2O shell in the as-prepared catalyst is favorable for the CO formation; while the CuO shell has poor selectivity for the CO production. A catalyst, composed of Cu2O and with a cubic shape, is also obtained. These Cu2O cubes show the highest activity for CO2RR and the best selectivity for CO production among all the prepared catalysts. Hence, by employing different catalysts, syngas with various H2/CO ratios can be easily obtained. Especially, a syngas with H2/CO ratio of 1-2 can be produced on the Cu2O cubes, which is suitable for further methanol synthesis. The observed syngas production rate is high at relatively positive potentials. These potentials also guarantee the syngas purity, avoiding the formation of multicarbon gas products. The present work highlights the importance of surface/subsurface chemistry of Cu-based catalysts for the CO2 electroreduction. By changing these properties, a syngas with desired characteristics can be obtained on low-cost Cu-based catalysts. This can be an indication for developing efficient and inexpensive electrocatalysts for large-scale production of syngas from the CO2 conversion.
